question:
A 16-year-old Caucasian boy presents to your family practice office complaining of itchiness. He denies other symptoms. He also denies tobacco, alcohol, or other illicit drug use and is not sexually active. He has no other significant past medical or surgical history aside from a meniscal repair from a wrestling injury sustained two years ago from which he has recovered fully. Vitals are T 98.3, HR 67, BP 110/70. On exam you note several pruritic, erythematous, slightly raised annular patches with central clearing on his back.

Which of the following additional tests or features are sufficient to make the diagnosis of this boy's skin lesion?

options.opa: Acid-fast bacilli on smear from skin scrapings
options.opb: History of recent herald patch and lesions along skin cleavage lines
options.opc: Presence of hyphae when KOH added to skin scrapings
options.opd: Symmetrical distribution on bilaterial extremities progressing proximally
options.ope: History of time spent in a Lyme-endemic region

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Pruritic, erythematous, annular patches with central clearing" -> "suggestive of tinea corporis" -> "KOH preparation shows hyphae" -> "diagnosis of tinea confirmed" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Pruritic, erythematous, annular patches with central clearing" -> "possible diagnosis of pityriasis rosea" -> "history of recent herald patch" -> "diagnosis of pityriasis rosea confirmed" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Pruritic, erythematous, annular patches with central clearing" -> "symmetrical distribution on bilateral extremities" -> "possible diagnosis of eczema or psoriasis" -> "requires further evaluation" -> 70%

CHAIN: "Pruritic, erythematous, annular patches with central clearing" -> "history of time spent in a Lyme-endemic region" -> "possible Lyme disease-related rash" -> "requires serological testing for confirmation" -> 60%

CHAIN: "Pruritic, erythematous, annular patches with central clearing" -> "acid-fast bacilli on smear from skin scrapings" -> "suggests possible mycobacterial infection" -> "not typical for presented lesions" -> "unlikely diagnosis" -> 40%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation of pruritic, erythematous, annular patches with central clearing is highly suggestive of tinea corporis, a fungal infection. The presence of hyphae when KOH is added to skin scrapings is a definitive test for confirming this diagnosis, aligning with standard medical consensus. The alternative diagnosis of pityriasis rosea could be considered if there was a history of a herald patch, but this is less likely without such a history. The symmetrical distribution on bilateral extremities could suggest other conditions like eczema or psoriasis, but these do not fit the described lesions as well as tinea corporis. The history of time spent in a Lyme-endemic region is not relevant to the diagnosis of the described skin lesions, and acid-fast bacilli on smear would indicate a mycobacterial infection, which is not typical for the lesions presented. Therefore, the most relevant and sufficient test to confirm the diagnosis is the presence of hyphae when KOH is added to skin scrapings.
analysis: The patient's presentation of pruritic, erythematous, annular patches with central clearing is characteristic of tinea corporis, a common fungal infection. The most definitive test for diagnosing tinea corporis is the identification of hyphae in skin scrapings when treated with KOH, which confirms the presence of a fungal infection. The other options do not provide sufficient evidence for the diagnosis: 'History of recent herald patch and lesions along skin cleavage lines' suggests pityriasis rosea, which is not indicated here; 'Symmetrical distribution on bilateral extremities progressing proximally' could indicate other dermatological conditions but does not confirm tinea; 'History of time spent in a Lyme-endemic region' is irrelevant to the skin lesions described; and 'Acid-fast bacilli on smear from skin scrapings' would indicate a mycobacterial infection, which is not consistent with the presentation. Therefore, the presence of hyphae when KOH is added to skin scrapings is the most appropriate and sufficient test to confirm the diagnosis of tinea corporis.
